units.title: Portability is a contract
units.problem: A utility builds on your laptop but fails on a production distribution. Which promise did the program actually depend on?
units.explanation: Separate the C language, the C library, the operating-system interface, and the kernel implementation. POSIX specifies observable behavior; Linux adds interfaces; glibc exposes wrappers and feature-test macros. A function appearing in a header does not prove that every deployment supports it. POSIX Issue 8 is the 2024 edition, not an alias for the older 2008 baseline.
units.contract: Define feature-test macros before any header. Use _POSIX_C_SOURCE=200809L when deliberately targeting that older interface set; _GNU_SOURCE requests GNU/Linux extensions in glibc. Check both compile-time availability and runtime failure where the kernel may lag behind the library.
units.pitfall: Calling an interface Linux-only forever because it originated on Linux can become inaccurate: dup3 entered POSIX.1-2024. A newer standard does not retroactively update an older operating system.
units.exercise: Compile a small declaration probe with strict warnings under two feature-macro settings. Record compiler, libc, kernel, and intended standard separately. A compile failure answers a declaration question, not a runtime-support question.

assessment.question: An API is in POSIX.1-2024. Does that guarantee it on an older POSIX.1-2008 system?
assessment.answer: No. Select a deployment baseline and provide a checked fallback or require an upgrade.
assessment.distractor: Yes. The POSIX name implies identical availability across editions.

worked.assumptions: glibc on Linux; source targets an older POSIX baseline.
worked.before: A declaration is hidden by feature-test macros.
worked.operation: Define the intended macro before headers and rebuild.
worked.observation: A declaration may become visible; runtime support still needs checking.
worked.tradeoff: A broader extension set simplifies Linux code but narrows portability.

units.title: Names, handles, and kernel objects
units.problem: A file is removed while a worker still reads it. Why does the worker continue?
units.explanation: A pathname is a lookup instruction. A descriptor is a small integer in one process. Its open file description carries state such as an offset and status flags. The underlying inode represents the file object. These are separate lifetimes: removing a directory entry does not invalidate an existing open reference.
units.contract: open returns a descriptor or -1. close releases that descriptor. unlink removes a name; storage can remain until the final link and final open reference disappear. A reused integer does not identify the old object.
units.pitfall: Logging only descriptor 7 across asynchronous operations can hide a reuse bug. After close, another open may return 7 for an unrelated file. Keep ownership explicit and do not let a delayed callback close a newly reused handle.
units.exercise: In a private temporary directory, open a file, unlink its name, then read through the open descriptor. Contrast that success with a new open of the removed pathname. Close the original descriptor to release the remaining reference.

assessment.question: Does unlink invalidate all descriptors already referring to the file?
assessment.answer: No. Open references survive removal of the directory entry.
assessment.distractor: Yes. A descriptor is only a cached pathname.

worked.assumptions: Regular file; one link; one open reference; calls succeed.
worked.before: notes has bytes OK and fd 3 points to its object.
worked.operation: unlink removes notes; read uses fd 3.
worked.observation: The old descriptor can read OK; a new open of notes fails.
worked.tradeoff: Handle-based work tolerates renames but retains resources until close.

units.title: Reading an API like a protocol
units.problem: A diagnostic prints an unrelated error even though the operation succeeded.
units.explanation: An API contract includes argument lifetime, success result, error representation, and side effects. errno is thread-local diagnostic state, not a global last-operation verdict. It is meaningful only when the function's documented result says an error occurred. Library calls can change it on success.
units.contract: Most system-call wrappers report -1 and set errno. Many pthread functions return an error number directly. Functions such as getpriority need special treatment because -1 can be a valid success result. Save errno immediately before cleanup that could overwrite it.
units.pitfall: A universal CHECK macro that assumes every nonzero result is an error will reject successful read byte counts and misreport pthread errors. Error conventions belong to individual interfaces.
units.exercise: Write two tiny wrappers: one for open and one for pthread_mutex_lock. Give each a deliberately invalid setup in a throwaway program and compare where the error number comes from. Do not unlock a mutex you did not acquire.

assessment.question: pthread_mutex_lock returns a nonzero error number. Where should the diagnostic obtain that number?
assessment.answer: From the return value, using the pthread API contract.
assessment.distractor: From errno, regardless of the function's return convention.

worked.assumptions: A pthread function returns EINVAL directly.
worked.before: errno contains an unrelated earlier error.
worked.operation: Store the pthread return value and pass it to strerror.
worked.observation: The diagnostic describes the actual pthread failure.
worked.tradeoff: Per-interface wrappers take more care than one universal error macro.

units.topic: File I/O: The Universal I/O Model
units.title: Byte transfer without wishful thinking
units.problem: A copy loop loses the tail of a file when a write transfers fewer bytes than requested.
units.explanation: read and write transfer bytes, not application records. A positive short result is progress. Advance the buffer by the returned count and keep the remainder. An empty pipe with writers is different from a pipe with no writers. A zero-count request is different again: its zero result is not evidence of EOF.
units.contract: For a positive read request on a regular file, zero means the current offset is at or beyond its current end; later growth can make data readable. For a stream, zero normally reports orderly end after buffered bytes drain. Noncanonical terminal reads and zero-length datagrams have additional zero-result meanings. EINTR before transfer is retryable when policy allows; EAGAIN means wait for readiness.
units.pitfall: Retrying every failure spins on permanent errors. Treating a positive short write as failure duplicates bytes if the entire buffer is resent. A successful write does not establish persistence on storage.
units.exercise: Run the descriptor lab and inspect the zero-count read beside a real read. Then implement a bounded copy of 17 bytes with a deliberately small three-byte buffer; verify exact output rather than the number of calls.

assessment.question: write returns 3 for a requested 8 bytes. What remains?
assessment.answer: The five bytes starting at buffer + 3; the first three were accepted.
assessment.distractor: All eight bytes, because short writes have no effect.

worked.assumptions: Eight-byte output; first write successfully transfers three bytes.
worked.before: Buffer contains ABCDEFGH; cursor is zero.
worked.operation: Advance cursor to three and request the remaining five.
worked.observation: The second request begins with D, avoiding a duplicate ABC.
worked.tradeoff: Explicit cursors add state but preserve partial progress.

units.title: Descriptor flags and shared offsets
units.problem: Two workers each write two bytes through duplicated descriptors. Will one overwrite the other?
units.explanation: dup creates another descriptor pointing to the same open file description. Offset and O_APPEND/O_NONBLOCK status belong to that shared description. FD_CLOEXEC belongs to each descriptor entry. A separate open of the same file creates a different description with an independent offset.
units.contract: dup clears close-on-exec on the new descriptor. dup3 with O_CLOEXEC requests it atomically. dup2 atomically replaces a target and, when both arguments are identical and valid, does nothing. pread and pwrite specify an offset without advancing the shared one; Linux pwrite with O_APPEND has a documented append caveat.
units.pitfall: For successful serialized writes through a shared description at offset zero, writing AB then CD yields ABCD, not CD overwriting AB. Concurrent order can vary; shared-offset atomicity is not a multi-call transaction. Two independent opens starting at zero can overwrite instead.
units.exercise: Use the descriptor model to duplicate fd 3, toggle close-on-exec on only fd 3, and execute a replacement image. Run descriptors.c to compare actual F_GETFD values and the resulting ABCD bytes.

assessment.question: fd 3 has FD_CLOEXEC. What does ordinary dup(3) give its new descriptor?
assessment.answer: A shared open file description, but a cleared close-on-exec flag.
assessment.distractor: An independent offset with the same close-on-exec flag.

worked.assumptions: Empty regular file; serialized successful calls.
worked.before: fd 3 has CLOEXEC and offset zero.
worked.operation: dup creates fd 4; write AB on 3 then CD on 4.
worked.observation: Bytes are ABCD; offset is four; fd 4 has CLOEXEC cleared.
worked.tradeoff: dup shares position; use a fresh open or positional I/O for independent position.

units.title: A process is more than a PID
units.problem: An exec trace shows the same PID executing two different programs. Is the trace corrupt?
units.explanation: A process combines a virtual address space, credentials, descriptors, signal state, and execution contexts. PID identifies the process within a PID namespace; it is not a permanent identity token. exec replaces a program image while retaining process identity. fork creates a child identity with inherited state.
units.contract: getpid returns the process ID and getppid its parent ID as visible in the namespace. argv and environ are user-space startup data. Changing a string in the environment does not alter the parent's environment. Successful execve does not return to the old program.
units.pitfall: PID reuse makes a delayed kill(pid, ...) unsafe as a stable ownership mechanism. Linux pidfds provide a handle-oriented alternative for supported operations. Multiple successful execve calls over a process lifetime are entirely possible.
units.exercise: Trace a shell that execs a small helper and compare PID before and after the replacement. Contrast it with a forked child. Treat the observed PID value as run-specific, not a fixed expected number.

assessment.question: Must a successful execve allocate a new PID?
assessment.answer: No. It replaces the calling process's program image.
assessment.distractor: Yes. Each executable image necessarily has a distinct PID.

worked.assumptions: A single process successfully execs an absolute path.
worked.before: PID P runs launcher with a local variable x.
worked.operation: execve replaces the image.
worked.observation: PID P remains; x and the old code no longer exist.
worked.tradeoff: Image replacement keeps selected resources but requires inheritance auditing.

units.title: Allocation, ownership, and address space
units.problem: A service allocates a huge buffer successfully and then dies while touching it.
units.explanation: malloc manages user-space allocations backed by a process address space. Virtual allocation, resident physical memory, and committed storage are different quantities. Linux overcommit can allow an allocation whose later page faults cannot all be satisfied. free ends the C object's lifetime, even if allocator caches keep pages mapped.
units.contract: Check multiplication before allocating count times element-size. On realloc failure the original nonzero-sized allocation remains valid; assign the result to a temporary pointer. Avoid zero-size realloc portability traps by spelling out free when the desired size is zero.
units.pitfall: A successful malloc is not a promise that a memory-intensive phase cannot hit resource or OOM limits. A stale pointer is invalid after free even if a debugger shows its old bytes. RSS not falling after free does not prove a leak.
units.exercise: Allocate only a bounded one-megabyte region, touch each page, and compare process maps and RSS before allocation, after touching, and after free. Expect allocator and kernel variation; do not attempt an OOM demonstration on a shared host.

assessment.question: realloc(p, larger_nonzero_size) returns NULL. What happens to p?
assessment.answer: The original allocation remains owned by the caller and must still be handled.
assessment.distractor: The original allocation was always freed by the failed call.

worked.assumptions: A nonzero realloc request fails.
worked.before: p owns a 64-byte allocation.
worked.operation: tmp = realloc(p, 128) yields NULL.
worked.observation: p still owns 64 bytes; reporting failure must not discard it.
worked.tradeoff: A temporary pointer costs one variable and prevents an ownership leak.

units.title: Identity databases are services
units.problem: A username lookup unexpectedly stalls a request path.
units.explanation: Numeric user and group IDs are kernel credentials. Human-readable names come from databases accessed through libc and NSS, potentially including network services. Reading /etc/passwd directly does not reproduce the configured lookup policy. A missing user and a lookup error are different outcomes.
units.contract: getpwnam_r uses caller-provided storage and a result pointer. A zero return with a NULL result means no matching entry; a nonzero return is an error number. ERANGE means the supplied buffer was too small. Bound growth and copy only fields whose lifetime you understand.
units.pitfall: Caching a pointer returned by a non-reentrant lookup can expose overwritten static storage. Assuming every account has a local password-file entry breaks managed environments. A primary group is not the complete supplementary-group set.
units.exercise: Look up the current numeric UID with getpwuid_r and compare it with a deliberately nonexistent name. Report not-found separately from failure; do not require access to shadow-password data.

assessment.question: getpwnam_r returns 0 and sets result to NULL. What does this mean?
assessment.answer: The lookup completed without finding that account.
assessment.distractor: A valid account exists and its fields are all empty.

worked.assumptions: NSS lookup succeeds operationally but the name is absent.
worked.before: Caller owns a result pointer and a bounded buffer.
worked.operation: getpwnam_r returns zero and result is NULL.
worked.observation: Report not found, without dereferencing result.
worked.tradeoff: System policy-aware lookup is broader than local parsing but can involve remote latency.

units.title: Credentials are authority, not labels
units.problem: A helper changes its effective UID but unexpectedly regains privilege later.
units.explanation: Real, effective, and saved IDs serve different purposes. Supplementary groups also contribute to authorization. Linux has filesystem IDs and capabilities as additional mechanisms. A temporary privilege switch differs from an irreversible drop. Ordering matters because changing UID can remove authority needed to change groups.
units.contract: setresuid and setresgid explicitly manipulate ID sets subject to privilege rules. For a dedicated privileged helper, establish the intended supplementary groups before permanently dropping group and user IDs, check every call, then verify the resulting authority. Exact capability behavior must be considered too.
units.pitfall: Ignoring a failed privilege-drop call is a security defect even when failure seems impossible. access checks using real IDs do not safely authorize a later open: pathname changes can race the two operations.
units.exercise: As an unprivileged user, print real/effective/saved IDs with getresuid on Linux. Attempt no root transition. Sketch a helper's ordered setup and explain what must happen if any step fails.

assessment.question: May a privileged helper continue normally after its required privilege drop fails?
assessment.answer: No. Abort the privileged operation and report the failed transition.
assessment.distractor: Yes. The subsequent file permissions will compensate for the failure.

worked.assumptions: A helper requires an irreversible authority drop.
worked.before: Supplementary groups still include a privileged group.
worked.operation: Attempt group setup before dropping user authority; check every result.
worked.observation: If required setup fails, abort the privileged operation.
worked.tradeoff: Permanent reduction limits damage but prevents later privileged work.

units.title: Choose the clock before the timestamp
units.problem: A timeout expires too late after the wall clock is adjusted.
units.explanation: Wall time answers calendar questions. Monotonic time answers elapsed-time questions without discontinuous wall-clock jumps. Linux CLOCK_BOOTTIME includes suspended time; CLOCK_MONOTONIC does not. CPU clocks measure execution consumption rather than waiting. A timestamp is incomplete without its clock domain.
units.contract: clock_gettime writes a timespec and returns 0 or -1. Normalize nanosecond arithmetic and avoid mixing clock domains. For deadlines, calculate an absolute target in the selected clock rather than repeatedly subtracting rounded relative sleeps.
units.pitfall: A monotonic clock need not measure suspend-inclusive time, and its values are not portable timestamps for exchange between machines. time_t width and the target ABI matter when storing long-lived calendar values.
units.exercise: Sample realtime, monotonic, and process CPU time around a short sleep. The CPU clock should advance much less than elapsed time, but no exact scheduler latency is guaranteed. Never change the system clock for this experiment.

assessment.question: Which clock is suitable for a local timeout that should ignore wall-clock jumps?
assessment.answer: A monotonic clock, with suspend behavior chosen deliberately.
assessment.distractor: A formatted local-time string, compared lexicographically.

worked.assumptions: Local timeout excludes machine suspension.
worked.before: Monotonic time is 20 seconds; timeout is 3 seconds.
worked.operation: Choose a monotonic deadline of 23 seconds.
worked.observation: A realtime clock adjustment does not move that deadline.
worked.tradeoff: Monotonic values support elapsed time but are not cross-machine timestamps.

units.title: Limits must be interpreted
units.problem: sysconf returns -1 and the program reports a bogus fatal error.
units.explanation: Limits can be compile-time minima, runtime system values, per-file values, or process resource ceilings. A standard minimum is not the current machine's capacity. Some queries permit an indeterminate limit. Resource limits and cgroup controls can both restrict a workload without being interchangeable.
units.contract: Set errno to zero before sysconf or pathconf when -1 can mean either indeterminate or error, then inspect errno only on that result. getrlimit exposes soft and hard limits; applications may generally lower their own soft limits but cannot assume authority to raise hard limits.
units.pitfall: Allocating a PATH_MAX-sized buffer and assuming every path fits is not a universal pathname strategy. A queried value can also change for some resource classes; correct code still handles operation failure.
units.exercise: Query _SC_OPEN_MAX and RLIMIT_NOFILE, then explain why neither tells you the number of descriptors currently open. Use a child process if experimenting with a lower limit so the parent shell remains unaffected.

assessment.question: sysconf returns -1 with errno still zero after you cleared it. Is this necessarily an error?
assessment.answer: No. For applicable queries it can report an indeterminate limit.
assessment.distractor: Yes. All negative results share the same errno contract.

worked.assumptions: The selected sysconf query permits an indeterminate result.
worked.before: errno is explicitly cleared.
worked.operation: sysconf returns -1 and errno remains zero.
worked.observation: Represent the limit as indeterminate, not a diagnosed syscall failure.
worked.tradeoff: Dynamic queries adapt to deployment but require richer result states.

units.title: Observing a moving process
units.problem: A monitoring script reads /proc/PID and finds inconsistent values across files.
units.explanation: procfs presents kernel state through file-like interfaces. A sequence of reads is not one global transaction: the process can allocate, exit, or exec between observations. Namespaces and permission checks affect visibility. A PID directory is not an immortal handle to a workload.
units.contract: Read bounded data, parse documented fields, and tolerate disappearing files. /proc/self refers to the reader itself. /proc/PID/fd exposes descriptor links subject to permissions; maps describes address mappings, not necessarily resident memory.
units.pitfall: Splitting /proc/PID/stat on spaces is unsafe because the parenthesized command name can contain spaces. Assuming every machine exposes the same fields or unrestricted process information makes diagnostics fragile.
units.exercise: Inspect /proc/self/status and maps from a small helper, then compare with /proc of a short-lived child. Classify ENOENT after child exit as a lifecycle observation rather than a corrupt filesystem.

assessment.question: Do two sequential procfs reads form a consistent process snapshot?
assessment.answer: No. State may change between reads; label the observation window.
assessment.distractor: Yes. procfs freezes the target until all open files are closed.

worked.assumptions: Target process may exit between observations.
worked.before: A status read succeeds for PID P.
worked.operation: The target exits before maps is opened.
worked.observation: ENOENT is a lifecycle race, not evidence that the first read was fabricated.
worked.tradeoff: Cheap snapshots are useful, but correlated monitoring needs timestamps and uncertainty.

units.title: Three stages of a write
units.problem: A log line appeared in memory but disappeared after a crash.
units.explanation: stdio can buffer bytes in user space. write can put bytes into the kernel's page cache. Persistence needs the relevant filesystem and device synchronization guarantees. fflush moves a stream's pending output toward its descriptor; it is not a storage-durability operation. Metadata and directory entries have their own persistence requirements.
units.contract: Check fflush and fclose results. For a durable replacement protocol on a suitable local filesystem, write a temporary file in the target directory, synchronize the file, rename it, and synchronize the directory. Failure handling must retain enough information for recovery; filesystem and hardware behavior still matter.
units.pitfall: fork copies unflushed user-space stdio buffers, so two later exit paths can flush duplicate output. Mixing stdio and raw descriptor I/O requires explicit coordination of buffering and offsets.
units.exercise: Print a line without a newline before fork in a bounded helper. Compare flushing before fork with letting both processes call exit. Repeat with output redirected to a file because terminal buffering can mask the effect.

assessment.question: Does fflush alone establish that bytes survive a power loss?
assessment.answer: No. It addresses the user-space stream buffer, not the full persistence path.
assessment.distractor: Yes. fflush is a portable equivalent of synchronizing a storage device.

worked.assumptions: Suitable local filesystem; all synchronization steps succeed.
worked.before: New bytes exist only in a stdio buffer.
worked.operation: Flush, synchronize the temporary file, rename, then synchronize the directory.
worked.observation: Each step advances a different buffering or namespace obligation.
worked.tradeoff: Durability adds latency; batching changes the acceptable loss window.

units.title: Filesystems as namespaces and storage
units.problem: rename works in one directory but fails when the destination is on another mount.
units.explanation: A filesystem organizes objects and names; the mount tree attaches filesystem instances into a namespace. A path crossing a mount point changes the backing filesystem. Free bytes, free inodes, quotas, reserved space, and mount policy can independently affect writes.
units.contract: rename provides an atomic namespace replacement within its supported scope but fails with EXDEV across mounted filesystems. statvfs exposes filesystem capacity information; available blocks can differ from total free blocks. Never equate a successful rename with crash durability.
units.pitfall: A copy-and-unlink fallback is not atomic and needs an explicit partial-failure policy. A nearly empty filesystem can still reject creation when an inode or quota limit is reached.
units.exercise: Inspect mount information and statvfs results without mounting anything. Design a cross-filesystem move protocol that labels the copy stage, verification stage, and source deletion stage. Explain what a crash leaves at each boundary.

assessment.question: Can copy followed by unlink preserve rename's atomic visibility across filesystems?
assessment.answer: No. Readers and crashes can observe intermediate states.
assessment.distractor: Yes. Two successful system calls always form one transaction.

worked.assumptions: Source and destination are on different mounted filesystems.
worked.before: Source is complete; destination is absent.
worked.operation: rename fails with EXDEV.
worked.observation: A copy fallback needs partial-copy cleanup and separate source deletion.
worked.tradeoff: Copy works across mounts but loses atomic move visibility.

units.title: Metadata is a snapshot
units.problem: A file passes a pathname permission check, then the opened object differs.
units.explanation: stat follows a pathname to metadata; lstat reports the symbolic link itself; fstat examines the already-open object. Permission bits include type-dependent meanings: directory execute grants search, while directory write controls changes to names subject to other rules. File write permission is not the same as permission to remove its name.
units.contract: Use S_ISREG and related macros to interpret mode types. umask masks requested creation permissions; it does not add permissions. Prefer checking an opened descriptor when the operation must refer to that same object. Timestamps can have filesystem-specific precision and update policy.
units.pitfall: stat followed by open is vulnerable to name replacement. Sticky directories add deletion restrictions, and ACLs or security modules can further change authorization. A mode-bit-only explanation is incomplete.
units.exercise: Create a file with requested mode 0666 in a private directory while a child uses umask 0077. Inspect the resulting mode and restore any modified process state. Compare fstat with lstat on a symlink.

assessment.question: With no default ACL, what permission bits result from mode 0666 and umask 0077?
assessment.answer: 0600: the mask removes group and other permissions.
assessment.distractor: 0777: umask adds the permissions named by the mask.

worked.assumptions: No default ACL; requested mode 0666; umask 0077.
worked.before: No file exists at a private test path.
worked.operation: Create the file successfully.
worked.observation: Permission bits are 0600, before any later chmod.
worked.tradeoff: A restrictive default prevents exposure but collaborators need deliberate grants.

units.title: Extended attributes are separate data
units.problem: A backup restores file contents but silently drops an application's metadata.
units.explanation: Extended attributes associate named byte values with filesystem objects. Namespaces such as user, trusted, security, and system carry different policy. Values are not necessarily text, and support depends on filesystem and mount configuration. Copying file bytes does not automatically copy these attributes.
units.contract: getxattr can first query a size, then retrieve the value. Another writer can change the size between calls, so handle ERANGE with bounded retries. Distinguish absence from unsupported operation and permission denial. The fgetxattr variant anchors access to an open object.
units.pitfall: Treating an attribute as a NUL-terminated string can overread binary data. Copying security attributes blindly across trust boundaries can be inappropriate even if the caller has permission.
units.exercise: On a disposable file, set a small user.lesson attribute, retrieve its exact byte length, and remove it. If the filesystem rejects the operation, record that as a capability result rather than fabricating output.

assessment.question: Is a size query followed by getxattr immune to concurrent changes?
assessment.answer: No. The second call must still handle a changed value size.
assessment.distractor: Yes. The first call reserves the attribute until retrieval.

worked.assumptions: An xattr writer races the reader.
worked.before: Size query reports four bytes.
worked.operation: The writer grows the value before retrieval.
worked.observation: Handle ERANGE with a bounded retry rather than trusting the stale size.
worked.tradeoff: Two-stage allocation avoids oversized buffers but requires race handling.

units.title: ACLs and the effective permission mask
units.problem: An ACL grants a named user write permission but the user still cannot write.
units.explanation: Linux POSIX-style access ACLs extend owner/group/other permissions with named users and groups. The ACL mask caps effective permissions for named users and the group class, but not the owning user or other entry. Default directory ACLs influence inheritance and are distinct from the directory's own access ACL.
units.contract: Use getfacl to inspect both requested and effective rights and setfacl only on disposable files. chmod can change the ACL mask through group-class bits. Linux POSIX ACLs reflect the historical draft model; do not claim that this interface is a mandatory POSIX.1-2024 feature.
units.pitfall: Looking only at one named entry misses the mask. A recursive permission change can unexpectedly alter effective rights inherited by a tree. Authorization also needs search permission on ancestor directories.
units.exercise: In an optional ACL-enabled filesystem lab, create a named-user entry with rw and a mask of r. Read getfacl's effective annotation. Do not modify another user's real files to perform this experiment.

assessment.question: A named user has rw, while the ACL mask is r. What is effective through that entry?
assessment.answer: Read only, because the mask caps the named-user entry.
assessment.distractor: Read and write, because a named entry bypasses the mask.

worked.assumptions: Named-user ACL entry rw; ACL mask r; ancestor search allowed.
worked.before: The named user attempts a write through that entry.
worked.operation: Intersect the entry with the mask.
worked.observation: Effective rights are r, so that entry does not authorize write.
worked.tradeoff: ACLs express fine-grained policy but require reviewing effective permissions.

units.title: Directory traversal without name races
units.problem: A recursive tool accidentally follows a symlink outside its intended tree.
units.explanation: A hard link is another directory entry for an inode; a symbolic link stores a path interpreted during lookup. Relative symlink targets are resolved relative to the link's containing directory. An open directory descriptor can anchor relative operations even when the working directory changes.
units.contract: openat takes a directory descriptor and a relative path; an absolute path ignores that descriptor. O_NOFOLLOW protects the final component, not every earlier component. Linux openat2 offers resolution constraints such as RESOLVE_BENEATH when a stronger traversal policy is required.
units.pitfall: readdir's d_type can be DT_UNKNOWN, so robust tools cannot require it to contain a type. readlink returns a byte count and does not append a terminating NUL. chdir is process-wide and can interfere with other threads.
units.exercise: Draw a tree with a relative symlink pointing to ../outside. Resolve it component by component. Compare a final-component O_NOFOLLOW policy with a beneath-root policy and identify which one rejects intermediate traversal.

assessment.question: Does O_NOFOLLOW alone forbid symlinks in every pathname component?
assessment.answer: No. Its ordinary open behavior concerns the final component.
assessment.distractor: Yes. It confines all traversal beneath the starting directory.

worked.assumptions: The final component is ordinary, but an earlier component is a symlink.
worked.before: root/link/file traverses link to an outside directory.
worked.operation: open uses only O_NOFOLLOW.
worked.observation: Final-component protection alone does not confine the entire lookup.
worked.tradeoff: openat2 resolution constraints are stronger but Linux-specific.

units.title: File events are hints to reconcile
units.problem: A directory watcher misses a rename during a burst of changes.
units.explanation: inotify places filesystem notifications in a bounded queue. Watches identify observed objects, and rename cookies help correlate move events, but the application must tolerate gaps and races. An event stream is a prompt to update a view of state, not an infallible audit log.
units.contract: Use inotify_init1 with appropriate nonblocking and close-on-exec flags. Parse each variable-length record using its reported length. Handle IN_Q_OVERFLOW by rebuilding the relevant state. Recursive trees require deliberate watch management because one directory watch is not recursive.
units.pitfall: Pairing rename events with an assumption of immediate adjacency fails under interleaving. A path can disappear before the consumer inspects it. Keeping only events without a reconciliation strategy makes overflow unrecoverable.
units.exercise: In a private directory, record create, rename, and delete activity. Then design a synthetic overflow input for your parser and verify that it requests a rescan rather than reporting a perfectly complete history.

assessment.question: What should a stateful watcher do after IN_Q_OVERFLOW?
assessment.answer: Reconcile against filesystem state and acknowledge that events were lost.
assessment.distractor: Continue treating the remaining queue as a complete change history.

worked.assumptions: A watcher maintains a cache of directory contents.
worked.before: The event queue overflows during a burst.
worked.operation: The consumer receives IN_Q_OVERFLOW.
worked.observation: Invalidate confidence in the event history and reconcile from the directory.
worked.tradeoff: Events are efficient for updates; rescans are the recovery path.

units.title: Signals: pending is not a message count
units.problem: A worker receives ten SIGUSR1 sends but handles fewer than ten notifications.
units.explanation: A standard signal has pending state, not an unbounded queue of occurrences. Repeated generation while the same standard signal is pending coalesces. Disposition is process-wide, while each thread has a signal mask. Blocking postpones delivery; ignoring selects a different disposition.
units.contract: Use sigaction to establish handling and pthread_sigmask for masks in threaded programs. SIGUSR1 and SIGTERM terminate by default; SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught or blocked. Real-time signals support queued instances within resource limits and have different ordering rules.
units.pitfall: A counter incremented by a handler cannot reliably count standard-signal sends. Unblocking a pending SIGTERM with its default disposition terminates the process; a teaching model must not silently treat it as a harmless callback.
units.exercise: Use the signal model to block SIGUSR1, generate it three times, then unblock. Compare a handler disposition with default termination. Run the bounded signals.c lab, which synchronously consumes a blocked signal without risking default delivery.

assessment.question: Three SIGUSR1 occurrences are generated while blocked and already pending. How many pending instances are represented?
assessment.answer: One standard-signal pending instance, not three queued messages.
assessment.distractor: Three guaranteed handler invocations in sending order.

worked.assumptions: SIGUSR1 is blocked; one process; no synchronous acceptance yet.
worked.before: No standard signal is pending.
worked.operation: Generate SIGUSR1 three times.
worked.observation: One pending instance exists; disposition decides what delivery does.
worked.tradeoff: Signals are light notifications; use queued IPC for counted work.

units.title: A signal handler interrupts invariants
units.problem: A handler logs through printf and occasionally deadlocks.
units.explanation: A handler can interrupt code while library internal state is halfway through an update. Ordinary thread safety is not sufficient for asynchronous interruption. The handler may reenter the same lock or allocator it interrupted. Keep its work minimal and hand control back to ordinary execution.
units.contract: Use only async-signal-safe operations in handlers. A volatile sig_atomic_t flag can communicate a simple condition to interrupted code under its defined constraints; it is not a general inter-thread synchronization primitive. Preserve errno when the handler makes calls that can change it.
units.pitfall: printf, malloc, and mutex locking are not general handler-safe tools. Checking a flag and then calling pause creates a lost-wakeup window. Block the signal while testing and use sigsuspend to atomically change the mask and wait.
units.exercise: Rewrite a handler that prints a message into one that sets a flag. Draw the arrival points between flag testing and sleeping, then remove the race with a blocked-mask/sigsuspend protocol.

assessment.question: Does marking a function thread-safe make it safe inside an asynchronous signal handler?
assessment.answer: No. Async-signal safety is a separate, stronger requirement.
assessment.distractor: Yes. Both properties simply mean a function uses locks.

worked.assumptions: A handler may interrupt a library call holding internal state.
worked.before: Main code is inside printf.
worked.operation: A handler calls printf again.
worked.observation: The reentry is not generally async-signal-safe; defer formatting to normal flow.
worked.tradeoff: Minimal handlers are easier to audit but need a handoff protocol.

units.title: Accepting signals synchronously
units.problem: A multithreaded server needs one place to handle shutdown signals.
units.explanation: Blocking a chosen set before creating threads causes those threads to inherit the mask. A dedicated waiter can then accept signals synchronously, where ordinary control flow is easier to reason about than asynchronous handlers. Linux signalfd integrates selected blocked signals with descriptor-based event loops.
units.contract: sigwait returns an error number directly, while sigwaitinfo returns a signal number or -1. Ensure the selected signals remain blocked in every thread that could otherwise receive them. Real-time queueing is bounded by resource policy; sigqueue can fail rather than queue forever.
units.pitfall: Creating workers before setting their inherited mask leaves a delivery window. Passing a pointer as a real-time signal value does not make that address meaningful in another process's address space.
units.exercise: Design a two-thread shutdown path: main blocks the set, creates a waiter and worker, waiter requests cooperative stop, main joins both. Include the case of repeated standard shutdown signals without assuming one event per send.

assessment.question: Why block the signal set before starting workers?
assessment.answer: New threads inherit the mask, preventing unintended asynchronous delivery there.
assessment.distractor: Blocking converts standard signals into reliable queued messages.

worked.assumptions: Shutdown set is blocked before pthread_create.
worked.before: The main thread establishes the mask.
worked.operation: Workers inherit it; one dedicated thread calls sigwait.
worked.observation: Shutdown can be handled in ordinary thread control flow.
worked.tradeoff: A waiter simplifies handlers but adds lifecycle coordination.

units.title: Timers schedule eligibility, not precision
units.problem: A periodic task drifts farther behind after each interrupted sleep.
units.explanation: A timer expiration makes work eligible; scheduler delays still affect when user code runs. Repeated relative sleeps include the duration of previous work and interruptions, causing drift. Absolute deadlines preserve the intended phase, but missed periods still require an application policy.
units.contract: clock_nanosleep with TIMER_ABSTIME can retry the same deadline after EINTR and returns an error number directly. timerfd exposes expiration counts through an eight-byte read on Linux. A count greater than one reports accumulated expirations, not repeated executions of your task.
units.pitfall: Calling the body once for every missed interval can create an unbounded catch-up storm. Skipping missed work may be better for telemetry but wrong for accounting. State the policy before choosing the loop.
units.exercise: Run timers.c for one short monotonic timerfd expiration. Extend it to three bounded periodic reads and add deliberately slow work in a local variant to inspect accumulated expiration counts. Do not assert an exact wakeup time or use a real-time scheduling policy.

assessment.question: An absolute sleep is interrupted. How can you preserve the original deadline?
assessment.answer: Retry with the same absolute target after handling EINTR.
assessment.distractor: Start a full relative interval again after every interruption.

worked.assumptions: Monotonic absolute deadline; clock_nanosleep interrupted before the target.
worked.before: Target is 5.000 seconds in the clock domain.
worked.operation: After handling EINTR, retry the same target.
worked.observation: Interruption does not add a fresh full interval.
worked.tradeoff: Fixed phase avoids drift but needs a missed-period policy.

units.title: Fork: copied state, shared references
units.problem: A child changes a variable, but the parent sees only a changed file offset.
units.explanation: fork creates a child with a logically separate address space, commonly implemented using copy-on-write. Descriptor tables are copied, but their entries refer to the same open file descriptions. This explains why ordinary variables diverge while file offsets can remain shared. Scheduling order is unspecified.
units.contract: fork returns the child PID in the parent, zero in the child, and -1 on failure with no child created. In a multithreaded parent, the child contains only the calling thread, while inherited memory may contain locks held by vanished threads. Restrict child work to async-signal-safe operations until exec.
units.pitfall: A sleep is not a synchronization protocol. Assuming the child runs first creates timing-dependent output. Calling complex library functions after a multithreaded fork can deadlock on inherited lock state.
units.exercise: Run processes.c. The child changes its copied integer to 9 and uses _exit(9); the parent retains 7 and decodes status 9. Extend only in a single-threaded local variant to compare a copied integer with a shared descriptor offset.

assessment.question: Does fork give the child an independent file offset for each inherited descriptor?
assessment.answer: No. The inherited entries reference the parent's open file descriptions.
assessment.distractor: Yes. Every inherited descriptor behaves like a fresh open.

worked.assumptions: Single-threaded parent; shared inherited descriptor; calls serialized.
worked.before: Parent integer is 7 and file offset is zero.
worked.operation: Child changes its integer to 9 and reads one byte.
worked.observation: Parent integer remains 7; shared file offset becomes one.
worked.tradeoff: fork isolates ordinary memory but shares some kernel references.

units.title: Exit has user-space and kernel phases
units.problem: A forked child unexpectedly emits its parent's buffered log line again.
units.explanation: Returning from main behaves like exit: registered cleanup and stdio flushing run in user space. _exit bypasses those user-space callbacks and buffers, while kernel teardown releases process resources. A terminated child can leave a waitable status until its parent reaps it.
units.contract: exit accepts an integer status whose low eight bits are available through the usual wait status interface. _exit is the appropriate failure path after exec fails in a restricted post-fork child. Closing descriptors during termination can still involve kernel work; immediate does not imply hard real-time completion.
units.pitfall: Calling exit after fork can duplicate a pre-fork stdio buffer or run cleanup intended only for the parent. A destructor is not a substitute for a durable storage protocol and will not run for every kind of termination.
units.exercise: Compare exit and _exit in a bounded single-threaded fork helper with redirected output. Flush before fork in the corrected version. Explain why neither mode guarantees recovery after SIGKILL or power failure.

assessment.question: Which child failure path avoids flushing inherited stdio buffers after exec fails?
assessment.answer: _exit with an explicit failure status.
assessment.distractor: exit, because it discards every inherited user-space buffer.

worked.assumptions: Single-threaded fork with an unflushed redirected stdio buffer.
worked.before: Parent's buffer contains one log prefix.
worked.operation: Both branches later call exit.
worked.observation: Each copied buffer may flush the prefix; flush before fork to avoid duplication.
worked.tradeoff: exit runs cleanup; _exit avoids inherited user-space cleanup in the restricted child.

units.title: Reaping is resource accounting
units.problem: A server handles SIGCHLD once but leaves several zombie children.
units.explanation: Child termination and parent observation are separate events. The kernel retains status for the parent to collect. Since standard SIGCHLD occurrences can coalesce, a signal tells the parent to inspect child state rather than counting exactly one termination.
units.contract: waitpid with WNOHANG returns a positive PID when a status was collected, zero when matching children exist but none is ready, or -1 on error. Decode status with WIFEXITED before WEXITSTATUS and WIFSIGNALED before WTERMSIG. A stopped child is not a terminated child.
units.pitfall: Calling waitpid only once per SIGCHLD can leave other children unreaped. Polling without a bound wastes CPU. Treat ECHILD distinctly from EINTR and ensure one component owns each child's wait lifecycle.
units.exercise: Run processes.c and verify child status 9. Design a draining waitpid(-1, ..., WNOHANG) loop that stops on zero or ECHILD, retries permitted EINTR, and records other failures. Do not interpret the packed status as the direct exit code.

assessment.question: waitpid with WNOHANG returns zero. What did it report?
assessment.answer: No requested child status is currently ready, not a successful reap.
assessment.distractor: A child with PID zero exited successfully.

worked.assumptions: One child exited with status 7; waitpid succeeds.
worked.before: Parent holds a packed wait status.
worked.operation: Check WIFEXITED, then WEXITSTATUS.
worked.observation: The decoded exit status is 7, not the raw packed integer.
worked.tradeoff: Explicit reaping retains diagnostics but requires clear wait ownership.

units.title: Exec is an image replacement boundary
units.problem: A helper inherits a database socket that its parent never intended to share.
units.explanation: execve replaces code, data, heap, and stack with a new image. Many process attributes survive, including identity and descriptors not marked close-on-exec. Caught signal dispositions reset, while ignored dispositions and the signal mask have specified inheritance behavior. Every inherited descriptor is a transfer of authority.
units.contract: execve accepts a path and NULL-terminated argv and envp vectors. On success it never returns; on ordinary failure it returns -1. Set close-on-exec at descriptor creation to avoid a race with another thread executing a new image. PATH-searching exec variants introduce a separate executable-resolution policy.
units.pitfall: Setting FD_CLOEXEC in a later fcntl can race a concurrent fork/exec. A sanitized argv does not sanitize the environment. Never treat a shell command string as equivalent to an argument vector for untrusted values.
units.exercise: Use the descriptor model's exec action to see which entries survive. In a Linux helper, pass only a small explicit environment and an absolute executable path; report exec failure through a pipe whose write end is close-on-exec.

assessment.question: What does reaching the next statement after execve normally tell you?
assessment.answer: The replacement failed, so inspect its failure result and errno.
assessment.distractor: The new program finished and control returned to the old image.

worked.assumptions: Successful exec; fd 3 CLOEXEC set; dup-created fd 4 clear.
worked.before: Both entries refer to one open file description.
worked.operation: Replace the program image.
worked.observation: fd 3 closes while fd 4 survives with the shared description.
worked.tradeoff: Atomic close-on-exec creation prevents leaks but inheritance must be deliberate.

units.topic: Process Creation and Program Execution in More Detail
units.title: Launching safely from a larger process
units.problem: A threaded application needs to launch a helper with redirected output.
units.explanation: A launch is a protocol: choose the executable, prepare descriptors, create the child, establish its environment, detect replacement failure, and collect termination. posix_spawn packages common setup through attributes and file actions, reducing the amount of custom post-fork code.
units.contract: posix_spawn returns an error number, not the usual -1/errno convention. A successful launch still requires waitpid to collect child completion. File actions are ordered; a close before a duplication can invalidate the source. system invokes a shell and has its own signal and status semantics.
units.pitfall: vfork is not a drop-in faster fork: the child shares constrained execution state until exec or _exit. Returning from the child path or modifying arbitrary data is unsafe. An implementation's fast path is not an application contract.
units.exercise: Write a launch plan for stdout redirection using posix_spawn file actions: open destination, duplicate to stdout if needed, close surplus handles, spawn, destroy actions, wait. Analyze the case where the opened descriptor already equals stdout.

assessment.question: Does a zero return from posix_spawn eliminate the need to wait for the child?
assessment.answer: No. Launch result and child termination status are separate observations.
assessment.distractor: Yes. The spawn call synchronously returns the helper's final exit status.

worked.assumptions: Spawn file actions redirect stdout; destination already happens to be fd 1.
worked.before: The destination descriptor equals the target descriptor.
worked.operation: Avoid an unconditional surplus-close action on fd 1.
worked.observation: The launched helper retains its intended stdout.
worked.tradeoff: Declarative spawn setup reduces post-fork code but action order still matters.

units.title: Threads share ownership problems
units.problem: A thread receives a pointer to a stack object that no longer exists.
units.explanation: Threads share address space and process resources but each has its own stack, execution state, and signal mask. Passing a pointer shares access, not lifetime management. The caller must keep the pointed-to object alive until the receiver is finished. Thread creation does not define which side executes first.
units.contract: pthread_create returns an error number and starts a function with signature void *(*)(void *). A joinable thread should be joined exactly once or detached. pthread_join establishes completion and retrieves the returned pointer; it does not make a pointer to a dead thread's stack valid.
units.pitfall: Passing the address of a changing loop variable to every worker gives them a race on one object. Leaking joinable thread resources is distinct from leaking heap memory. Use pthread_equal rather than assuming a portable integer representation for pthread_t.
units.exercise: Run threads.c with two bounded workers and one shared mutex-protected counter. Each worker receives stable storage. Verify the final total after both joins instead of guessing the interleaving from print order.

assessment.question: May a thread safely return a pointer to its automatic local variable for the joiner to use?
assessment.answer: No. Its automatic storage lifetime ends with the thread's function.
assessment.distractor: Yes. pthread_join extends every object on the terminated thread's stack.

worked.assumptions: Two workers each increment 1000 times under one mutex.
worked.before: Shared counter starts at zero; argument storage survives both joins.
worked.operation: Join both successfully completed workers.
worked.observation: The final counter is 2000 regardless of scheduling order.
worked.tradeoff: Locking gives correctness but can serialize a hot counter.

units.title: Synchronization protects a predicate
units.problem: A worker wakes from a condition wait although the queue is still empty.
units.explanation: A mutex protects the invariant of shared state. A condition variable lets a thread wait until that state may have changed. Notification is not stored work, and waking does not prove the predicate is true. Another consumer may win the mutex first, or a spurious wakeup may occur.
units.contract: pthread_cond_wait atomically releases the associated mutex while waiting and reacquires it before returning. Test the predicate in a while loop under that mutex. Writers update the predicate under the same synchronization discipline and then notify as appropriate. Use a global lock order to prevent cycles.
units.pitfall: Replacing while with if can consume nonexistent work. Holding a mutex while performing unbounded network I/O can serialize the entire service. Robust mutex EOWNERDEAD requires state repair and pthread_mutex_consistent, not blind success handling.
units.exercise: Trace two consumers and one queued item: both wake, one consumes, the second reacquires later. Write the predicate value at each lock boundary. Run the counter lab to distinguish data-race prevention from scheduling order.

assessment.question: After pthread_cond_wait returns, may a consumer assume the queue is nonempty?
assessment.answer: No. Recheck the protected predicate in a loop.
assessment.distractor: Yes. Each signal transfers ownership of one queue item.

worked.assumptions: Two consumers, one queued item, shared mutex and predicate.
worked.before: Both consumers are awakened.
worked.operation: First consumes; second reacquires the mutex later.
worked.observation: Second sees empty and waits again in its while loop.
worked.tradeoff: Predicate loops tolerate contention and spurious wakes at the cost of retesting.

units.topic: Threads: Thread Safety and Per-Thread Storage
units.title: Thread-local storage is not object isolation
units.problem: A supposedly thread-safe helper returns a pointer that changes after a later call.
units.explanation: Thread safety describes allowed concurrent use, not necessarily independent result storage. Reentrancy is another property. Thread-local storage supplies one value per thread, useful for error state and caches, but any pointers stored there may still refer to shared objects.
units.contract: pthread_key_create creates a key shared across threads; pthread_setspecific assigns that thread's value. A destructor can release per-thread heap storage on thread exit subject to destructor iteration rules. C thread-local objects have storage semantics distinct from heap ownership.
units.pitfall: Deleting a pthread key does not automatically free all values stored by existing threads. A thread-local pointer to a global mutable buffer does not remove the underlying race. Static-result functions can invalidate earlier pointers even in a single thread.
units.exercise: Design a formatter whose caller supplies a buffer, then compare it with one returning thread-local storage. State whether two consecutive calls in the same thread can retain both results. Make the lifetime part of the API documentation.

assessment.question: Does making a pointer thread-local make the shared object it points to thread-local too?
assessment.answer: No. Pointer storage and pointed-to object ownership are separate.
assessment.distractor: Yes. The runtime automatically clones the object for each thread.

worked.assumptions: One thread stores a pointer to a shared global buffer in thread-local storage.
worked.before: A second thread holds another pointer to that same buffer.
worked.operation: Both modify the pointed-to bytes without synchronization.
worked.observation: Thread-local pointer variables do not remove the shared-data race.
worked.tradeoff: Caller-owned buffers make ownership clearer than hidden reusable storage.

units.title: Cancellation is an unwinding protocol
units.problem: A canceled worker leaves a mutex locked and the process hangs.
units.explanation: Cancellation is a request whose delivery depends on state, type, and cancellation points. Deferred cancellation is easier to reason about than asynchronous cancellation, which can strike while almost any invariant is broken. Cooperative stop flags often provide a clearer application lifecycle.
units.contract: pthread_cancel requests cancellation; it does not join the thread or prove completion. Cleanup handlers run on cancellation and can release acquired resources when correctly paired. pthread_cleanup_push/pop may be macros requiring matching lexical scope. Disable cancellation around short critical ownership transitions when necessary.
units.pitfall: Installing cleanup before acquiring a mutex can attempt an invalid unlock on another path. Forgetting that pthread_cond_wait reacquires the mutex before cancellation cleanup can produce a leak. Async cancellation makes most ordinary library operations unsafe.
units.exercise: Draw ownership states for acquire, install cleanup, wait, remove cleanup, release. Choose a disciplined ordering that covers each cancellation point. Prefer a cooperative bounded worker in runnable examples rather than trying to demonstrate undefined behavior.

assessment.question: Does pthread_cancel returning zero prove the target has exited?
assessment.answer: No. Join or another explicit completion protocol is still required.
assessment.distractor: Yes. Cancellation always synchronously destroys the target thread.

worked.assumptions: Deferred cancellation; thread is waiting on a condition variable.
worked.before: The wait released its mutex.
worked.operation: Cancellation occurs and the wait reacquires the mutex before cleanup.
worked.observation: An installed cleanup handler can release that owned mutex.
worked.tradeoff: Cooperative stop is often clearer; cancellation requires audited cleanup boundaries.

units.title: Thread attributes and finite resources
units.problem: A service creates thousands of threads and fails well before exhausting physical RAM.
units.explanation: Each thread needs stack address space and runtime/kernel resources. Default stack size, guard regions, resource limits, and cgroup limits affect capacity. Detaching changes resource reclamation after termination; it does not make a running thread free. Affinity constrains placement but does not grant exclusive CPU access.
units.contract: Initialize pthread attributes, set requested values with error checks, pass them to pthread_create, and destroy the attribute object afterward. A caller-supplied stack has its own lifetime and guard responsibilities. Linux affinity APIs are extensions with dynamically sized CPU sets on large machines.
units.pitfall: Choosing a tiny stack based on one call path can fail with deeper recursion, signals, or library changes. Treat EAGAIN as a capacity outcome requiring backpressure, not an invitation to spin creating more threads.
units.exercise: Inspect default attributes using the available platform interfaces and calculate a bounded pool budget. Include per-task queue memory as well as thread stacks. Explain why a fixed worker pool still needs a bounded admission queue.

assessment.question: Does detaching a live thread immediately release its stack and execution resources?
assessment.answer: No. Reclamation happens after that thread terminates.
assessment.distractor: Yes. Detached execution requires no per-thread resources.

worked.assumptions: Illustrative pool of 32 threads, each configured with a 1 MiB stack.
worked.before: Queue memory has not yet been included.
worked.operation: Calculate 32 MiB of stack address space alone.
worked.observation: This is not total RSS or total service memory; add queues and runtime overhead.
worked.tradeoff: Smaller stacks save address space but increase overflow risk.

units.topic: Process Groups, Sessions, and Job Control
units.title: Job control separates sessions and groups
units.problem: Pressing Ctrl-C terminates a pipeline's workers rather than only the shell's immediate child.
units.explanation: A process group collects related processes for signaling and terminal job control. A session contains process groups and may have a controlling terminal. The terminal's foreground process group receives terminal-generated signals. Parent-child structure and process-group membership are different relationships.
units.contract: setpgid establishes process-group membership subject to session and lifecycle constraints. setsid creates a new session when permitted; a process-group leader cannot simply call it successfully. tcsetpgrp selects a foreground group under terminal rules. kill with a negative group ID targets a group.
units.pitfall: A background process reading its controlling terminal can receive SIGTTIN. Treating process groups as security boundaries is incorrect. Shell launch code often sets group membership in both parent and child to close scheduling races.
units.exercise: Inspect PID, PPID, PGID, SID, and terminal foreground group for a harmless shell pipeline. Draw two separate trees: ancestry and group membership. Do not send group signals to a shell you need to keep running.

assessment.question: Is a process group necessarily identical to a parent and all of its descendants?
assessment.answer: No. Membership is explicitly managed within session constraints.
assessment.distractor: Yes. Fork ancestry permanently determines every process group.

worked.assumptions: Foreground terminal group contains both workers of a pipeline.
worked.before: Shell is a different process group.
worked.operation: Terminal receives its configured interrupt character with ISIG enabled.
worked.observation: SIGINT targets the foreground group rather than just one immediate child.
worked.tradeoff: Groups simplify job control but are not security isolation.

units.title: Scheduling promises and weighted shares
units.problem: A team expects nice 10 to mean exactly ten percent CPU.
units.explanation: Nice values influence relative weights for ordinary scheduling, not fixed CPU percentages. Under simplified equal-group, one-CPU contention, Linux nice 0 has weight 1024 and nice 5 has weight 335, yielding roughly 75% versus 25% between those two continuously runnable tasks. Cgroups, affinity, sleeping, and load balancing change real outcomes.
units.contract: Linux began replacing CFS task selection with EEVDF in kernel 6.6. EEVDF uses eligibility and virtual deadlines rather than a promise that the smallest raw runtime always runs next. Real-time policies have different rules and can starve ordinary work if misused. getpriority needs errno disambiguation for a valid -1 result.
units.pitfall: A browser weight calculator is not a scheduler emulator. Ratios between nice levels are approximately multiplicative, not a linear subtraction from 100%. Kernel-version-specific details should not be presented as timeless POSIX requirements.
units.exercise: Compute 1024/(1024+335) and identify every assumption needed to interpret it as a share. Compare the historical CFS documentation with current EEVDF documentation. Do not run unbounded real-time loops as a lab.

assessment.question: Does nice 5 promise five percent less CPU than nice 0?
assessment.answer: No. Nice changes relative weights; actual shares depend on competing runnable work and policy.
assessment.distractor: Yes. Nice is defined as a linear percentage allocation.

worked.assumptions: One CPU, two continuously runnable ordinary tasks, same group, weights 1024 and 335.
worked.before: Total weight is 1359.
worked.observation: Approximate shares are 75.35% and 24.65%; this is not an EEVDF execution trace.
worked.tradeoff: Weights express relative preference, not absolute CPU reservations.

units.title: Resource limits are failure inputs
units.problem: An accept loop repeatedly fails because the process has no descriptor slots left.
units.explanation: Resource limits cap selected process resources; cgroups impose additional group-level policy. Soft and hard limits differ, and inherited limits shape helper programs. Usage counters describe accumulated work or high-water marks, not necessarily instantaneous utilization.
units.contract: getrlimit/setrlimit inspect and adjust limits under privilege rules. RLIMIT_NOFILE bounds descriptor-number allocation and can produce EMFILE. getrusage reports CPU time and other counters; ru_maxrss is a maximum, with platform-specific units. Linux reports it in kilobytes.
units.pitfall: Retrying accept immediately on EMFILE can create a hot error loop. A reserved descriptor strategy may help reject a pending connection, but admission control and leak diagnosis are still required. Raising limits without memory budgeting moves the failure elsewhere.
units.exercise: In a child only, lower a descriptor limit to a modest bound and open /dev/null until failure, retaining handles for cleanup. Count successful opens rather than assuming the limit equals new capacity; standard and inherited descriptors already occupy slots.

assessment.question: Does RLIMIT_NOFILE equal the number of additional files a process can always open?
assessment.answer: No. Existing descriptors and other system constraints affect available capacity.
assessment.distractor: Yes. It excludes every descriptor already present.

worked.assumptions: Child has a low RLIMIT_NOFILE and already-open standard descriptors.
worked.before: The numeric limit is 16.
worked.operation: Repeated new opens reach EMFILE before 16 additional successes.
worked.observation: Existing slots consume part of the budget.
worked.tradeoff: Limits contain damage but require backpressure and error handling.

units.title: Services need a lifecycle contract
units.problem: A supervisor thinks a daemon exited even though a detached grandchild is still running.
units.explanation: Traditional daemonization detached from a terminal and adjusted working directory, masks, and descriptors. A modern supervisor commonly expects a foreground process whose lifetime it can track directly. Startup, readiness, liveness, shutdown, and restart are separate lifecycle events.
units.contract: setsid detaches session relationships subject to its constraints. umask is process-wide. chdir and descriptor closure must be deliberate, preserving logging and control channels. A shutdown handler should request ordinary control flow to stop accepting work, drain within a deadline, and release resources.
units.pitfall: Blind double-forking under a foreground supervisor obscures process ownership. Closing every descriptor can destroy an intentionally inherited activation socket. A PID file alone is subject to stale contents and PID reuse.
units.exercise: Specify a foreground worker's lifecycle: initialize, bind, declare ready, accept bounded work, stop admission, drain, exit. For each state, define what an external supervisor should observe. Use no background orphan process in the lab.

assessment.question: Should every supervised service double-fork by default?
assessment.answer: No. Match the supervisor's foreground and readiness contract.
assessment.distractor: Yes. Detachment is mandatory for every long-running process.

worked.assumptions: Supervisor expects one foreground service process.
worked.before: Worker initializes but has not yet bound its socket.
worked.operation: Publish readiness only after initialization and binding succeed.
worked.observation: Process existence and service readiness are different observations.
worked.tradeoff: Foreground supervision simplifies ownership; readiness still needs a protocol.

units.title: Privileged code narrows its inputs
units.problem: A privileged helper opens a path after checking it, but an attacker swaps a directory entry.
units.explanation: Authority amplifies ordinary bugs. Treat paths, environment variables, inherited descriptors, locale, arguments, and working directory as inputs. Reduce privileged operations to a narrow phase, use handle-based operations where possible, and make ownership explicit before dropping authority.
units.contract: Use atomic creation with O_EXCL or a suitable temporary-file API in a trusted directory. openat2 can constrain Linux path resolution. Never use access followed by open as an authorization transaction. Avoid invoking a shell to interpret untrusted text and check every credential transition.
units.pitfall: Sanitizing only the filename leaves environment-driven loader or program behavior unaddressed. A symlink check can itself race. Logging a secret or privileged file's content during error handling can create a second vulnerability.
units.exercise: Threat-model a helper that replaces one configuration file. Enumerate trusted directory handles, accepted relative names, allowed modes, inherited descriptors, and the point of irreversible privilege drop. Test rejection paths unprivileged.

assessment.question: Does checking a pathname with access make a later open race-free?
assessment.answer: No. Resolve and operate on a securely acquired object instead.
assessment.distractor: Yes. The kernel reserves the checked path for the next call.

worked.assumptions: An adversary can replace a pathname between two operations.
worked.before: access approves the current object.
worked.operation: The entry changes before open.
worked.observation: The later operation can address another object; the check was not a reservation.
worked.tradeoff: Directory-handle-based operations reduce name races but require explicit policy.

units.title: Capabilities divide privilege, imperfectly
units.problem: A service gets CAP_SYS_ADMIN to solve one error and gains far more authority than intended.
units.explanation: Linux capabilities split traditional root powers into sets associated with threads and executable files. Effective, permitted, inheritable, bounding, and ambient sets participate in transitions. A capability is meaningful within user-namespace and target-resource rules; it is not a universally scoped permission token.
units.contract: Inspect capabilities before and after exec and UID changes rather than assuming they survive unchanged. no_new_privs constrains privilege gain across exec. File capabilities require filesystem support and deployment review. Prefer the narrow capability actually needed over broad administrative authority.
units.pitfall: Dropping one effective bit may leave permitted authority that can restore it. Containers and user namespaces alter the scope of apparent privilege. CAP_SYS_ADMIN covers many unrelated operations and is rarely a minimal default.
units.exercise: Read /proc/self/status capability masks and map only the bits you need using capabilities(7). Write a transition table for launch, setup, and steady state. Do not grant capabilities to the lab binaries just to make a demonstration succeed.

assessment.question: Does clearing only an effective capability always make the privilege permanently unrecoverable?
assessment.answer: No. Other sets and transition rules can allow it to become effective again.
assessment.distractor: Yes. Effective and permitted sets are merely two names for the same state.

worked.assumptions: A capability remains in a thread's permitted set.
worked.before: Its effective bit is cleared.
worked.operation: The program later attempts to make it effective again.
worked.observation: Clearing only effective authority need not make the reduction permanent.
worked.tradeoff: Capabilities narrow authority better than blanket root, but transition rules are complex.

units.title: Login records are accounting, not authority
units.problem: A tool treats a login-record entry as proof that a user is currently authenticated.
units.explanation: utmp-style records describe login and session accounting conventions. They are mutable records maintained by cooperating programs, not a complete authoritative view of every process or authentication event. Containers, remote services, and graphical sessions may not fit a simple terminal-login model.
units.contract: Use documented utmpx interfaces and respect fixed-size fields that may not be NUL-terminated. Record timestamps and terminal names are data requiring validation. Do not edit the system accounting database for an educational experiment; work with a private copy or synthetic record.
units.pitfall: Assuming every active user has a record can omit sessions. Assuming every record is fresh can count stale sessions. Binary layouts and time-field widths can vary by ABI, so raw structs are a poor cross-machine interchange format.
units.exercise: Create a synthetic bounded record decoder that prints fixed-size fields with explicit lengths. Explain how you would distinguish no record, stale record, and a permission failure without presenting any of them as authentication proof.

assessment.question: Is a utmp entry sufficient evidence to authorize a privileged operation?
assessment.answer: No. Accounting records are not an authentication or authorization decision.
assessment.distractor: Yes. A recorded username is a kernel-verified bearer credential.

worked.assumptions: A synthetic fixed-width username field has no terminating NUL.
worked.before: The decoder receives exactly the record's documented field length.
worked.operation: Print with an explicit bound rather than scanning as an unlimited C string.
worked.observation: No bytes beyond the field are consumed.
worked.tradeoff: Binary accounting is compact but ABI-dependent and not proof of authentication.

units.title: Shared objects and ABI boundaries
units.problem: A library update links successfully but crashes an old application.
units.explanation: A shared library supplies code and data through an application binary interface: symbol names, calling conventions, object layouts, and lifecycle rules. Source compatibility does not imply binary compatibility. The static linker records dependencies, and the runtime loader resolves them when the process starts or loads more objects.
units.contract: Build position-independent shared objects with the toolchain's supported flags and assign an intentional SONAME for ABI compatibility. Export only the intended interface. The dynamic loader's search rules involve recorded paths, configuration, and environment, with secure-execution restrictions.
units.pitfall: Changing a public structure layout can break callers compiled against the old layout even if function names stay unchanged. Relying on the current working directory for library lookup is fragile and potentially unsafe.
units.exercise: Design a library API around an opaque handle and explicit create/destroy functions. Compare that with exporting the whole structure. Inspect dependency and symbol tables of a local binary using readelf rather than executing an untrusted binary with diagnostic tooling.

assessment.question: Does preserving exported function names alone guarantee ABI compatibility?
assessment.answer: No. Calling conventions, layouts, semantics, and ownership also form the ABI.
assessment.distractor: Yes. Dynamic linking validates all caller and callee type information.

worked.assumptions: Old caller compiled against a public struct with two fields.
worked.before: New library inserts a field before the second one.
worked.operation: Caller and library use different offsets for the same member.
worked.observation: Symbol lookup can succeed while binary behavior is broken.
worked.tradeoff: Opaque handles limit layout coupling at the cost of accessor calls.

units.title: Runtime loading needs an ownership protocol
units.problem: A plugin is unloaded while another thread is still calling one of its functions.
units.explanation: dlopen adds an object to a runtime linking environment. dlsym resolves a symbol; dlclose releases a loader reference. Application references to functions and objects are a separate lifetime problem. Loader reference counting does not know whether an arbitrary thread retained a function pointer.
units.contract: Clear dlerror before dlsym and inspect dlerror afterward because a NULL symbol value alone does not universally identify an error. Choose RTLD_NOW versus RTLD_LAZY and symbol visibility deliberately. Establish a versioned plugin entry point and a stop/join/destroy protocol before closing the handle.
units.pitfall: Calling through a saved pointer after unload can jump into unmapped or reused memory. Passing allocator-owned objects across incompatible runtimes can break deallocation. RTLD_GLOBAL can expose symbols to unrelated later loads and create hidden coupling.
units.exercise: Specify a plugin ABI with a version, structure size, function table, and host-provided callbacks. Trace shutdown: reject new calls, finish outstanding calls, free plugin objects through the owning API, then close the loader reference.

assessment.question: Can a loader reference count prove that no worker still holds a function pointer?
assessment.answer: No. The application must coordinate outstanding calls and pointer lifetimes.
assessment.distractor: Yes. dlclose automatically discovers and waits for every saved pointer.

worked.assumptions: A worker retains a plugin function pointer.
worked.before: Loader reference count is about to drop to zero.
worked.operation: Host first blocks new calls, joins outstanding work, and destroys owned plugin objects.
worked.observation: Only then can the application safely release its loader reference.
worked.tradeoff: Unloading saves resources but greatly complicates pointer lifetimes.

units.title: Choose an IPC contract before an API
units.problem: Two processes share a memory region but disagree about whether a job is complete.
units.explanation: Communication needs a data format, an ownership rule, a notification mechanism, and a failure policy.
